n. 1918 · United Kingdom and Canada

Brenda Milner

British-Canadian neuropsychologist. Her study of the patient H. M. showed that memory depends on specific brain regions and that there are several distinct memory systems.

Biography

Brenda Langford Milner was born in Manchester in 1918. Her father, a music critic, taught her at home until she was eight. She first studied mathematics at Cambridge but switched to experimental psychology, training in Frederic Bartlett's laboratory. During the Second World War she worked on research for the British armed forces.

In 1944 she moved to Montreal with her husband. She took her doctorate at McGill University under Donald Hebb and began working at the Montreal Neurological Institute with the neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield, who operated on patients with epilepsy. She spent her whole career there, and went on researching and coming to the institute well past the age of ninety.

Questions she investigated

  • Which mental functions are lost when a specific part of the brain is damaged?
  • Where are new memories formed?
  • Is memory a single capacity or several?

Contributions

In 1953 the neurosurgeon William Scoville removed part of both temporal lobes, including the hippocampus, from a patient, Henry Molaison, known as H. M., to treat severe epilepsy. The epilepsy improved, but H. M. lost the ability to form new conscious memories. In 1957 Scoville and Milner published the case: it was the first clear evidence that the hippocampus is essential for memory.

Milner asked H. M. to trace a star while looking only at its reflection in a mirror, a difficult task. Over three days he improved like anyone else, although each time he said he had never done it before. She thus showed that there is a procedural memory for skills that works without the hippocampus, distinct from declarative memory for facts and events. She also studied the functions of the frontal lobe, such as the ability to switch strategy, and differences between the two hemispheres of the brain.

Collaborations, influences and disagreements

Her work connects the Cambridge experimental tradition, through Bartlett, with Donald Hebb's ideas about the brain and learning, and with Wilder Penfield's neurosurgery. Her findings opened the way for the cognitive neuroscience of memory, later developed by researchers such as Larry Squire and Suzanne Corkin.

A documented anecdote

Milner studied H. M. for decades, but he never remembered her: every time they met, she had to introduce herself again. Henry Molaison died in 2008 and his brain was cut into thousands of slices to study it in detail.

Criticism, limits and reception

The H. M. case has the limits of any single-patient study, and his lesion turned out to be somewhat different from the one first described. But the findings have been confirmed in many other patients and with neuroimaging. Milner received, among other honours, the Balzan Prize in 2009 and the Kavli Prize in Neuroscience in 2014.

References

  1. Scoville, W. B. y Milner, B. (1957). Loss of recent memory after bilateral hippocampal lesions. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry, 20(1), 11–21.
  2. Milner, B., Squire, L. R. y Kandel, E. R. (1998). Cognitive neuroscience and the study of memory. Neuron, 20(3), 445–468.
  3. Corkin, S. (2013). Permanent present tense: The unforgettable life of the amnesic patient, H. M. Nueva York: Basic Books.
